Oklahoma's Sweepstakes Casino Ban Takes Effect November 1

Published October 9, 2026 · 4 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

Players on sweepstakes casino platforms in Oklahoma have until November 1 to withdraw their funds and close out their accounts. SB 1589, which bans the dual-currency sweepstakes casino model statewide, takes effect that day after the state legislature overrode Governor Kevin Stitt's veto earlier this year — a fight that pitted the governor against both chambers and against the state's tribal gaming interests, who backed the bill heavily.

How the bill got here

SB 1589 passed the Oklahoma Senate unanimously, 48-0, in early March, then cleared the House with 65 votes in early May. Stitt vetoed it on May 7, calling the bill "vague and overbroad" in his veto message and warning it would "criminalize everyday apps people use for fun" — reportedly citing an online retailer's promotional spin-the-wheel discount offer as an example of something the bill's language could theoretically sweep up. He also objected to the bill creating a new felony and extending criminal liability to businesses and service providers rather than just operators. The legislature wasn't persuaded: the Senate voted to override 34-10, and the House followed with a 68-19 override vote about a week after the veto.

What the law actually does

Once SB 1589 takes effect, sweepstakes casino platforms — which let players use free "Gold Coin" currency for fun alongside redeemable "Sweeps Coin" currency, a structure operators have used nationwide to argue they aren't legally gambling — must exit Oklahoma entirely. Violations carry a Class C2 felony charge, with fines between $500 and $2,000 and the possibility of imprisonment, and that criminal liability isn't limited to the platforms themselves: it extends to payment processors, geolocation providers, gaming suppliers, and even media affiliates that promote the sites. The law carves out exemptions for tribal gaming conducted on tribal land under the federal Indian Gaming Regulatory Act, and for nonprofit charitable gaming under Oklahoma's existing Charity Games Act.

Why it matters beyond Oklahoma

The veto fight doubled as a proxy battle over Oklahoma's tribal gaming politics — Stitt, in his final year in office under term limits, has a long record of friction with the state's tribes, which strongly supported the ban. The Social Gaming Leadership Alliance, a trade group that lobbies against sweepstakes-casino restrictions in multiple states, has reportedly pointed to Stitt's "overbroad" veto language as unexpected validation for its own arguments elsewhere, even though it lost this particular fight. Oklahoma now joins a growing list of states that have moved against the sweepstakes casino model over the past two years, adding pressure on an industry already facing legal challenges from state attorneys general elsewhere in the country.
